Okay, so you have been invited to dinner at somebody's house here. Let me tell you what nobody tells newcomers. Rule one: RSVP, and do it fast. If the invitation says RSVP by Wednesday, the host is planning the food around your answer, so a maybe is honestly worse than a no. Rule two: if you have a dietary restriction, say it when you RSVP, not at the table. Rule three: never arrive with empty hands. A bottle of wine, flowers, a dessert. If it is a potluck, the host will tell you what to bring, and if they say just bring yourself, bring something small anyway. Rule four: seven o'clock means seven fifteen. Never early, because the host is still in the shower. And here is the one that surprises everybody from Brazil. When the host says help yourself, they mean it. Nobody is going to fill your plate three times. If you want seconds, you get up and take them. Oh, and dinners here end early. Around ten, somebody says, well, this was lovely, and that is your signal to go home.

Hi Gisele, it's Raj from 4B, across the hall. Thank you so much for the invitation, that's really kind of you. So, yes, we'd love to come to the housewarming on Saturday. That's me, my wife Anjali and our daughter, so three of us, if that's okay. Two quick things. We don't eat beef, so that's our only dietary restriction. Chicken and fish are completely fine. And I know the invitation says no need to bring anything, but Anjali makes a very good mango dessert, and she is going to bring it whether you like it or not. So please don't make a dessert. Oh, and if you need extra chairs, we have two folding ones. I can drop by on Friday after work and leave them with you. Okay, call me back, or just text me. See you Saturday.

Here is my opinion, after twenty years of having people over. Stop apologizing. Every host does it. Sorry, the apartment is small. Sorry, the rice is a little dry. Sorry, I'm not a real cook. And every time you apologize, your guests have to stop and say, no, no, it's perfect. You are giving them a job. Your job as a host is not perfection. It is attention. Notice the empty glass and offer a refill. Notice the person who is quiet and ask them a question. Would you like some more? Shall I open a window? That's the whole skill. And here is the secret nobody believes. People do not remember the food. They remember how they felt at the table. The best dinner I ever went to was soup and bread in a kitchen with four chairs and six people. So cook one thing you know, put it on the table, and say, please, help yourself. Then sit down and enjoy your own party.
